The biochemical goal of treatment is to nor- malise growth hormone and IGF-I concentrations in order to reduce some of the signs and symptoms of acromegaly and to reverse the increased risk of mortality.2 Growth hormone is usually measured after an oral glucose tolerance test (OGTT); this suppresses growth hormone concentrations in healthy subjects, but not in patients with acromegaly. A growth hormone concentration below 1 microgram/litre after an OGTT may be used to exclude acromegaly at the initial diagnosis, and as a target in the assessment of treatment efficacy in acromegaly. Growth hormone concentrations taken as random samples or as mean 24-hour measures may also be used during the long- term monitoring of patients treated for acromegaly; in such circumstances a target concentration below 2.5 micrograms/litre is often used.3 However, the target concentrations that have been suggested have changed over time with the development of more sensitive assays, and results must be interpreted in the context of the method used.4 Random IGF-I concentrations should be reduced to normal for age and sex.3,5 As for most pituitary tumours, surgery is the mainstay of treatment.2,5 The success rate depends on surgical exper- tise and the size and extension of the mass, with success rates higher for microadenomas (about 80%) than mac- roadenomas (less than 50%) depending on criteria.3,6 Drug therapy for acromegaly is indicated for patients who refuse surgery, are at increased risk from surgery, have active disease after surgery, or are awaiting the effects of radiotherapy (see below).2 The somatostatin analogues, octreotide and lanreotide, reduce growth hormone secre- tion in most patients, but not all will have persistent sup- pression and normalisation of growth hormone levels.7,8 Reported response rates vary, but effective growth hor- mone suppression occurs in about 50 to 55% of patients, and IGF-I is normalised in about 50 to 65%. Somatostatin analogues also produce tumour shrinkage, reducing tumour size by 20 to 50% in about 30% of patients, and improve signs and symptoms of acromegaly, including improvements in cardiac structure and function. Octre- otide and lanreotide are given as sustained-release intra- muscular injections.7 Octreotide may be more effective than lanreotide, but not all formulations have been com- pared.8 Octreotide can also be given by subcutaneous in- jection, but must be given three times daily, making it less attractive for long-term therapy.
